papers.title: DRAFT: graph-recurrent learning of dynamic gene regulatory networks along single-cell multi-omics trajectories
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767145 v1

summary.one_liner: Single-cell multi-omics data offer an opportunity to resolve how gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are rewired during cell-fate transitions, but most existing methods infer static snapshots, ignore temporal dependencies or assume linear regulation.

papers.abstract: Single-cell multi-omics data offer an opportunity to resolve how gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are rewired during cell-fate transitions, but most existing methods infer static snapshots, ignore temporal dependencies or assume linear regulation. Here we present DRAFT, a deep learning framework that combines graph attention with recurrent temporal memory to infer dynamic GRNs from time-resolved single-cell multi-omics data. On simulated data, DRAFT outperforms existing methods in accuracy and temporal smoothness. In mouse cellular reprogramming and Drosophila adult spermatogenesis, it recovers interactions supported by independent ChIP-seq, perturbation and Hi-C data, together with known stage-specific regulators. By inferring regulatory activity from dynamic network structure rather than expression alone, DRAFT identifies regulators whose activity precedes their transcriptional peak, including the candidate early germline regulator Mondo. Germline-specific Mondo knockdown alters germline stem cell number and expression of the predicted targets kuz and mamo. DRAFT also enables nonlinear alignment of co-developing lineages and reveals stage-specific cell-cell communication.

papers.title: Gene regulatory networks and the organization of cell differentiation in multicellular organisms
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767571 v1

summary.one_liner: Across their development, clonal multicellular organisms generate new cell types from less differentiated cell types.

papers.abstract: Across their development, clonal multicellular organisms generate new cell types from less differentiated cell types. Differentiation pathways arrange into a hierarchical, tree-like organization: regressions from specialized to undifferentiated cell types rarely occur and undifferentiated cell types often have the potential to produce, when subject to distinct stimuli, two or more differently specialized cell types. How cell type transitions acquire such a peculiar disposition requires an explanation that must reside in the properties of gene regulatory networks (GRNs); after all, GRNs orchestrate the changes in gene activity that define cell types. We studied vast numbers of small dynamic model networks to search for elementary GRNs that could yield the simplest hierarchical, developmental-like, differentiation patterns. We found that only a small minority of GRNs are compatible with hierarchical cell type transitions. Importantly, GRNs that yielded developmental-like differentiation patterns shared common traits: One is the presence of tangles of cycles of positive interactions. Genes in such a tangle produce an all-or-none one-way response to a signal. Another such trait is mutual inhibition between genes associated to different specialized cell types, enforcing their mutually exclusive activation. Moreover, these regulatory patterns are more abundant in published experimentally sustained developmental GRNs than as expected by chance. In addition, we show that it is easy to maintain hierarchical cellular differentiation throughout evolution, even when undergoing changes in gene regulatory interactions and developmental mechanisms. Our work supports the prevalence of design principles that organize hierarchically differentiation pathways in clonal multicellular organisms.

papers.title: Breadth over Depth: Predictor-Agnostic Consensus for Improved Antibody--Antigen Structure Prediction
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767212 v1

summary.one_liner: Antibody-antigen structure prediction commonly relies on sampling a single co-folding predictor deeply and selecting its highest-confidence output using model-specific confidence scores.

papers.abstract: Antibody-antigen structure prediction commonly relies on sampling a single co-folding predictor deeply and selecting its highest-confidence output using model-specific confidence scores. We introduce AbPoolRank, a predictor-agnostic structural selector that ranks mixed pools using cross-pose agreement, within-source reproducibility and interface geometry, without native confidence, predictor identities or predictor-specific parameters. On 103 cluster-disjoint, post-2021 antibody-antigen complexes from SAbDab2, three structures each from Boltz-2, Promera, Protenix-v2, ESMFold2-Fast and OpenDDE form a 15-structure pool that reaches 58.0% medium-or-better Success@1 (DockQ [≥] 0.49), exceeding confidence-based selection from every individual predictor sampled 100 times (26-52%). Existing ranking methods did not rescue deep single-predictor sampling or surpass our selector on mixed pools, with no method exceeding 51.5% on 100 structures from one co-folder and AbPoolRank matching the strongest single-structure methods while significantly outperforming consensus methods. AbPoolRank trained without one predictor lost at most 3.0 percentage points, and the frozen model accepted full MSA-conditioned ESMFold2, a sixth predictor absent from method development, without retraining or loss of accuracy. Diversification also improved the accuracy-compute frontier, with the 15-structure pool using 1.8-fold less aggregate GPU time than the most accurate single-predictor setting in our compute benchmark and 3.3-fold less than sampling that predictor 100 times. Together, these results show that shallow sampling across complementary co-folders, coupled with a confidence-free selector, provides an accurate and computationally efficient inference strategy for antibody-antigen structure prediction.
